title: About
text: This is the complete reference documentation for ComplexHeatmap-py, a faithful Python port of the R/Bioconductor ComplexHeatmap package (upstream R version 2.25.3). Examples throughout this book are generated under complexheatmap 0.2.0 backed by NumPy, SciPy, pandas, and Matplotlib. ComplexHeatmap-py Library (GitHub): https://github.com/zhanxw/ComplexHeatmap-py Figure Gallery (All 416 Plots): Browse Figure Gallery Book Source & Scripts (GitHub): https://github.com/zhanxw/ComplexHeatmap-reference-py

title: Installation
text: Install the latest release from PyPI or directly from https://github.com/zhanxw/ComplexHeatmap-py: pip install ComplexHeatmap-py Or install from source on GitHub: git clone https://github.com/zhanxw/ComplexHeatmap-py.git cd ComplexHeatmap-py pip install -e . In Python scripts and notebooks, import the package using: import complexheatmap as ch from complexheatmap import Heatmap, HeatmapAnnotation, colorRamp2, draw, gpar, unit ComplexHeatmap-py mirrors the R ComplexHeatmap API closely so existing workflows translate nearly line-for-line. Like its R predecessor—which was originally inspired by pheatmap—ComplexHeatmap-py provides familiar argument names and even includes a drop-in ch.pheatmap() translator (see Chapter 10) that maps pheatmap arguments directly onto a composable Heatmap object.

title: 1 Introduction
text: Complex heatmaps are efficient for visualizing associations across multiple sources of data sets and revealing potential patterns. ComplexHeatmap-py (https://github.com/zhanxw/ComplexHeatmap-py) provides a highly flexible, object-oriented framework in Python to arrange multiple heatmaps and support rich built-in as well as self-defined annotation graphics.

title: 1.1 General design
text: A single heatmap is composed of the heatmap body and surrounding heatmap components. The heatmap body can be split by rows and columns into multiple slices. The heatmap components are titles, dendrograms, row/column names or labels, and heatmap annotations, which can be placed on any of the four sides of the heatmap body. All heatmap components are automatically reordered or split according to the heatmap body. Conceptual layout of a single heatmap A heatmap list (HeatmapList) is the concatenation of a list of heatmaps and standalone heatmap annotations. Surrounding the heatmap list, there are global-level titles and packed heatmap/annotation legends. One central design principle of a horizontal heatmap list is that rows across all heatmaps and row annotations are adjusted simultaneously so that the same row in every heatmap and annotation corresponds to the exact same feature. Conceptual layout of a horizontal HeatmapList Heatmaps and column annotations can also be concatenated vertically (using %v% or /), in which case columns across all heatmaps and column annotations are aligned to the same samples or observations. Conceptual layout of a vertical HeatmapList A heatmap list can likewise be split by rows (in horizontal mode) or by columns (in vertical mode) according to the main heatmap. ComplexHeatmap-py mirrors the object-oriented class hierarchy of the R package: Heatmap: represents a single heatmap containing the matrix body, row/column names, titles, dendrograms, and attached top/bottom/left/right annotations. HeatmapList: represents a horizontal (+) or vertical (%v% / /) list of heatmaps and standalone HeatmapAnnotation objects, together with global titles and legends. HeatmapAnnotation: defines a stack of row annotations (rowAnnotation(...) or which="row") or column annotations (HeatmapAnnotation(...) or which="column"). Annotations can serve as components of a Heatmap or stand independently inside a HeatmapList. Several lower-level classes power color mapping and custom graphics: SingleAnnotation: defines a single row or column annotation track; a HeatmapAnnotation holds a collection of SingleAnnotation objects. ColorMapping: manages continuous (colorRamp2) and discrete (dict) mappings from data values to colors and constructs the corresponding legend grobs. AnnotationFunction: wraps user-defined Python drawing callbacks so custom vector/raster graphics automatically scale, align, and subset alongside heatmap slices. Under the hood, ComplexHeatmap-py implements an R-compatible grid graphics subsystem backed by Matplotlib (Viewport, pushViewport, popViewport, seekViewport, unit, gpar, grid.rect / grid_rect, grid.text / grid_text, grid.segments / grid_segments, grid.points / grid_points, grid.polygon / grid_polygon, grid.circle / grid_circle, and grid.raster / grid_raster). Notice in Python that ComplexHeatmap-py positions viewports explicitly via nested Viewport(x=..., y=..., width=..., height=..., just=...) coordinates rather than grid.layout. Understanding basic Viewport, unit(), and gpar() calls unlocks the full power of cell_fun, layer_fun, custom annotations, and post-draw decorations.

title: 2 A Single Heatmap
text: A single heatmap is the most widely used visualization for matrix data. Although the signature strength of ComplexHeatmap-py lies in aligning a list of multiple heatmaps and annotations in parallel, each single Heatmap serves as the fundamental building block, so configuring it well is essential. First, let’s generate a synthetic 18 × 24 pandas.DataFrame containing three row groups and three column groups, with rows and columns randomly shuffled: import numpy as np import pandas as pd import complexheatmap as ch from complexheatmap import Heatmap, colorRamp2, draw, gpar, unit rng = np.random.default_rng(123) nr1, nr2, nr3 = 4, 8, 6 nc1, nc2, nc3 = 6, 8, 10 nr = nr1 + nr2 + nr3 nc = nc1 + nc2 + nc3 b1 = np.vstack([ rng.normal(1.0, 0.5, (nr1, nc1)), rng.normal(0.0, 0.5, (nr2, nc1)), rng.normal(0.0, 0.5, (nr3, nc1)), ]) b2 = np.vstack([ rng.normal(0.0, 0.5, (nr1, nc2)), rng.normal(1.0, 0.5, (nr2, nc2)), rng.normal(0.0, 0.5, (nr3, nc2)), ]) b3 = np.vstack([ rng.normal(0.5, 0.5, (nr1, nc3)), rng.normal(0.5, 0.5, (nr2, nc3)), rng.normal(1.0, 0.5, (nr3, nc3)), ]) mat = np.hstack([b1, b2, b3]) mat = mat[np.ix_(rng.permutation(nr), rng.permutation(nc))] mat = pd.DataFrame( mat, index=[f"row{i + 1}" for i in range(nr)], columns=[f"column{j + 1}" for j in range(nc)], ) Calling Heatmap(mat) with only the matrix creates a Heatmap with default settings, and calling draw(ht) (or ht.draw()) renders dendrograms, row/column names, and a continuous blue-white-red color legend: ht = Heatmap(mat) draw(ht) Default single heatmap By default, the legend title is taken from the name of the heatmap. Each heatmap has a name acting as a unique identifier, which becomes important when concatenating multiple heatmaps or referencing a heatmap in decorate_* calls. When name is omitted, an automatic internal name of the form matrix_%d is assigned. Throughout the remaining examples in this chapter, we pass name="mat". Because Heatmap() is a lazy constructor (see Section 2.11), in Python scripts or inside loops and functions you should explicitly call draw(ht) or ht.draw() (passing save="heatmap.png" to write directly to disk): for item in matrices: ht = Heatmap(item, name="mat") draw(ht, save="out.png")

title: 2.1 Colors
text: For continuous numeric matrices, colors are typically controlled by a continuous color mapping function generated by colorRamp2(breaks, colors). It accepts a vector of breakpoints and a matching sequence of colors, linearly interpolating inside every interval in CIE LAB color space by default and clamping values outside the breakpoint range. Using colorRamp2() also ensures the legend displays clean, meaningful ticks. In the example below, values between -2 and 2 are interpolated from green through white to red, while values above 2 map to pure red and values below -2 map to pure green: col_fun = colorRamp2([-2, 0, 2], ["green", "white", "red"]) col_fun(np.arange(-3, 4)) # ['#00FF00FF', '#00FF00FF', '#B1FF9AFF', '#FFFFFFFF', '#FF9E81FF', '#FF0000FF', '#FF0000FF'] draw(Heatmap(mat, name="mat", col=col_fun)) Heatmap with colorRamp2 mapping Notice two key properties of colorRamp2(): 1. Negative values always map cleanly to green and positive values to red, centered at 0. 2. Color mapping is robust to outliers. Adding an extreme value (mat2.iloc[0, 0] = 100000 using 0-based indexing) dramatically alters clustering but leaves the color scale intact: mat2 = mat.copy() mat2.iloc[0, 0] = 100000.0 draw(Heatmap(mat2, name="mat", col=col_fun, column_title="a matrix with outliers")) Heatmap with an extreme outlier More importantly, sharing one col_fun across multiple heatmaps guarantees identical value-to-color correspondence across plots: draw(Heatmap(mat, name="mat", col=col_fun, column_title="mat")) draw(Heatmap(mat / 4.0, name="mat", col=col_fun, column_title="mat / 4")) draw(Heatmap(np.abs(mat), name="mat", col=col_fun, column_title="abs(mat)")) Comparing multiple heatmaps with the same colorRamp2 If you pass a plain list of colors to col for a continuous matrix, ComplexHeatmap-py linearly interpolates from min(mat) to max(mat). Keep in mind that a raw color sequence is sensitive to outliers: import matplotlib rainbow_cols = [ matplotlib.colors.to_hex(matplotlib.colormaps["rainbow"](x)) for x in np.linspace(1.0, 0.0, 10) ] draw(Heatmap(mat, name="mat", col=rainbow_cols, column_title="set a color vector for a continuous matrix")) Continuous matrix with a color sequence When the matrix holds discrete values (numeric or string), supply a Python dict mapping each value to its color, which automatically produces a discrete legend. For discrete integer matrices, keys can be integers or strings: rng = np.random.default_rng(123) discrete_mat = rng.integers(1, 5, size=(10, 10)) colors = {1: "black", 2: "#DF536B", 3: "#61D04F", 4: "#2297E6"} draw(Heatmap(discrete_mat, name="mat", col=colors, column_title="a discrete numeric matrix")) Discrete numeric matrix heatmap For character/string matrices, pass a dictionary mapping each category string to a color (or an R palette integer 1..8): discrete_char = rng.choice(["a", "b", "c", "d"], size=(10, 10)) colors_char = {"a": "black", "b": "#DF536B", "c": "#61D04F", "d": "#2297E6"} draw(Heatmap(discrete_char, name="mat", col=colors_char, column_title="a discrete character matrix")) Discrete character matrix heatmap Notice that numeric matrices enable row and column clustering by default (for both continuous and discrete colors), whereas character matrices disable clustering by default unless a custom clustering object or distance function is supplied (see Section 2.3.1). Missing values (np.nan or None) are supported and rendered with na_col (default "grey"). Matrices containing NaN can still be clustered using pairwise complete observations as long as no pair of rows or columns lacks finite overlapping entries. NA values are omitted from the legend: mat_with_na = mat.mask(rng.choice([True, False], size=mat.shape, p=[0.1, 0.9])) draw(Heatmap(mat_with_na, name="mat", na_col="black", column_title="a matrix with NA values")) Heatmap containing missing values Color interpolation depends heavily on the color space. colorRamp2() defaults to "LAB", while "RGB", "sRGB", "XYZ", and "HSV" are also supported: brks =

title: 2.2 Titles
text:
Row and column titles describe the heatmap and can be placed on "left"/"right" (row_title_side) or "top"/"bottom" (column_title_side). Visual styling is configured via row_title_gp and column_title_gp using gpar(), and horizontal/vertical orientations are set via row_title_rot and column_title_rot: Heatmap(mat, name="mat", column_title="I am a column title", row_title="I am a row title") Heatmap(mat, name="mat", column_title="I am a column title at the bottom", column_title_side="bottom") Heatmap(mat, name="mat", column_title="I am a big column title", column_title_gp=gpar(fontsize=20, fontface="bold")) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", row_title="row title", row_title_rot=0) Basic row and column title configurations Titles also act as templates when rows or columns are split (see Section 2.7): # Produces slice titles cluster_1 and cluster_2 Heatmap(mat, name="mat", row_km=2, row_title="cluster_%s") To draw a colored background and border box behind a title, set fill and border inside row_title_gp or column_title_gp (col sets the text color). Extra vertical padding around boxed titles can be adjusted via ht_opt.TITLE_PADDING. Mathematical notation works through Matplotlib mathtext strings (r"$...$"), and multi-style HTML/Markdown formatting is supported via gt_render(): from complexheatmap import gt_render, ht_opt ht_opt.TITLE_PADDING = unit([8.5, 8.5], "points") draw( Heatmap( mat, name="mat", column_title="I am a column title", column_title_gp=gpar(fill="red", col="white", border="blue"), ) ) ht_opt(RESET=True) draw(Heatmap(mat, name="mat", column_title=r"$\hat{\beta} = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y$")) draw( Heatmap( mat, name="mat", column_title=gt_render( "**Blue bold** / *italic*
" "Large rich-text title", r=unit(2, "pt"), padding=unit([3, 4, 3, 4], "pt"), ), ) ) Boxed, mathematical, and gt_render rich-text column titles

title: 2.3 Clustering
text: ComplexHeatmap-py supports flexible hierarchical clustering configured via: - Pre-defined distance metrics (e.g., "euclidean", "pearson", "spearman"). - Custom 1-argument matrix distance functions or 2-argument pairwise vector distance functions. - Pre-computed Hclust, Dendrogram, or SciPy linkage objects. - Custom clustering functions returning Hclust, Dendrogram, or linkage arrays. General clustering visibility, side placement, and dendrogram dimensions are controlled by: Heatmap(mat, name="mat", cluster_rows=False) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", show_column_dend=False) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", row_dend_side="right", column_dend_side="bottom") Heatmap(mat, name="mat", column_dend_height=unit(3, "cm"), row_dend_width=unit(3, "cm")) General dendrogram and clustering visibility/side options

title: 2.3.1 Distance methods
text: clustering_distance_rows and clustering_distance_columns accept: 1. Built-in distance strings supported by ch.dist(): "euclidean", "maximum" ("chebyshev"), "manhattan" ("cityblock"), "canberra", "binary" ("jaccard"), "minkowski", plus correlation distances "pearson", "spearman", and "kendall" (computed as (1 - corr) / 2 handling NaN pairwise). 2. A 1-argument function fn(m) computing a DistMatrix from a matrix m (column matrices are transposed automatically before calling fn). 3. A 2-argument function fn(x, y) returning a scalar distance between two 1D vectors (internally wrapped by ch.dist2()). Using a custom pairwise distance function makes clustering robust against extreme outliers: mat_with_outliers = mat.copy() for i in range(10): mat_with_outliers.iloc[i, i] = 1000.0 def robust_dist(x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> float: qx = np.quantile(x, [0.1, 0.9]) qy = np.quantile(y, [0.1, 0.9]) mask = (x > qx[0]) & (x < qx[1]) & (y > qy[0]) & (y < qy[1]) xs, ys = x[mask], y[mask] return float(np.sqrt(np.sum((xs - ys) ** 2))) col_fun = colorRamp2([-2, 0, 2], ["green", "white", "red"]) draw(Heatmap(mat_with_outliers, name="mat", col=col_fun, column_title="euclidean dist")) draw( Heatmap( mat_with_outliers, name="mat", col=col_fun, clustering_distance_rows=robust_dist, clustering_distance_columns=robust_dist, column_title="robust_dist", ) ) Default Euclidean vs robust trimmed pairwise distance on outliers A character matrix can also be clustered once a pairwise distance function is provided: mat_letters = rng.choice(["a", "b", "c", "d"], size=(10, 10)) def dist_letters(x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> float: ax = np.array([ord(str(c)) for c in x], dtype=float) ay = np.array([ord(str(c)) for c in y], dtype=float) return float(np.sqrt(np.sum((ax - ay) ** 2))) draw( Heatmap( mat_letters, name="letters", col={"a": 2, "b": 3, "c": 4, "d": 5}, clustering_distance_rows=dist_letters, clustering_distance_columns=dist_letters, cell_fun=lambda j, i, x, y, w, h, col: ch.grid_text(mat_letters[i, j], x, y), column_title="clustering a character matrix", ) ) Clustering a character matrix with a custom ASCII distance

title: 2.3.2 Clustering methods
text: Hierarchical linkage methods ("complete", "single", "average", "ward.D", "ward.D2", "mcquitty", "median", "centroid") are chosen via clustering_method_rows and clustering_method_columns. You can also pass pre-computed Hclust / Dendrogram / SciPy linkage arrays, a clustering function fn(m) returning an Hclust or Dendrogram, or cluster_within_group() / cluster_between_groups() to restrict clustering to known subgroups: from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import fcluster from complexheatmap import cluster_within_group, dist, hclust hc_r = hclust(dist(mat), method="ward.D2") hc_c = hclust(dist(mat.T), method="average") grp = [f"G{k}" for k in fcluster(hc_c.linkage, 3, criterion="maxclust")] Heatmap(mat, name="mat", clustering_method_rows="single") Heatmap(mat, name="mat", cluster_rows=hc_r, cluster_columns=hc_c) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", cluster_columns=cluster_within_group(mat.to_numpy(), grp)) Clustering linkage methods, pre-computed Hclust, and cluster_within_group If fastcluster is installed, you can enable accelerated linkage globally via ht_opt.fast_hclust = True.

title: 2.3.3 Render dendrograms
text: ch.color_branches(dend, k=...) colors subtree branches across k clusters. Setting row_dend_gp or column_dend_gp overrides branch colors globally. In Python, per-node markers can be added directly on Dendrogram nodes via node.node_par: from complexheatmap import as_dendrogram, color_branches row_dend = color_branches(as_dendrogram(hclust(dist(mat))), k=2) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", cluster_rows=row_dend) # Global gpar overrides branch colors Heatmap(mat, name="mat", cluster_rows=row_dend, row_dend_gp=gpar(col="red")) # Add node symbols via node_par def style_nodes(node): node.node_par = {"pch": 16, "col": "#377EB8", "size": unit(2.2, "mm")} for child in node.children: style_nodes(child) Colored dendrogram branches, row_dend_gp override, and custom node markers

title: 2.3.4 Reorder dendrograms
text: By default (row_dend_reorder=True when cluster_rows is boolean or a function, False when an explicit Hclust/Dendrogram is given), branches at internal nodes are rotated according to negative row/column means (reorder_dendrogram) to place dissimilar features farther apart. Passing a numeric vector to row_dend_reorder or column_dend_reorder supplies custom leaf weights: m2 = np.arange(1, 101).reshape(10, 10) draw(Heatmap(m2, name="mat", row_dend_reorder=False, column_title="no reordering")) draw(Heatmap(m2, name="mat", row_dend_reorder=True, column_title="applied reordering")) Effect of row_dend_reorder on a sequential 10x10 matrix

title: 2.4 Set row and column orders
text: Row and column orders can be fixed manually via row_order and column_order using either 0-based integer indices or row/column label names. Setting row_order automatically turns off row clustering (cluster_rows=False), and similarly for column_order: # 0-based numeric ordering matching row1..row18 and column1..column24 r_idx = np.argsort([int(r.replace("row", "")) for r in mat.index]) c_idx = np.argsort([int(c.replace("column", "")) for c in mat.columns]) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", row_order=r_idx, column_order=c_idx, column_title="reorder by numeric index") Heatmap(mat, name="mat", row_order=sorted(mat.index), column_order=sorted(mat.columns), column_title="reorder by row/column names") Manual row and column ordering by 0-based indices and by names Remember the distinction: row_dend_reorder rotates subtrees without changing the dendrogram topology, whereas row_order imposes a fixed sequence and disables hierarchical clustering.

title: 2.5 Seriation
text: Seriation seeks a linear leaf ordering that places similar profiles adjacent to one another. In Python, scipy.cluster.hierarchy.optimal_leaf_ordering computes an optimal leaf ordering directly on a hierarchical clustering linkage and condensed distance matrix, which wraps cleanly back into ch.Hclust and ch.as_dendrogram(): from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import optimal_leaf_ordering d_r = dist(mat) d_c = dist(mat.T) hc_r = hclust(d_r) hc_c = hclust(d_c) z_opt_r = optimal_leaf_ordering(hc_r.linkage, d_r.condensed) z_opt_c = optimal_leaf_ordering(hc_c.linkage, d_c.condensed) hc_opt_r = ch.Hclust(z_opt_r, n=mat.shape[0], labels=list(mat.index), method=hc_r.method) hc_opt_c = ch.Hclust(z_opt_c, n=mat.shape[1], labels=list(mat.columns), method=hc_c.method) # Order only (no dendrograms) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", row_order=hc_opt_r.order, column_order=hc_opt_c.order) # Optimal-leaf-ordered dendrograms Heatmap(mat, name="mat", cluster_rows=as_dendrogram(hc_opt_r), cluster_columns=as_dendrogram(hc_opt_c)) Heatmap seriation via SciPy optimal_leaf_ordering

title: 2.6 Dimension labels
text: By default, row names appear on the "right" and column names on the "bottom". Side placement, visibility, font styling, centering, and rotation can all be customized: Heatmap( mat, name="mat", row_names_side="left", row_dend_side="right", column_names_side="top", column_dend_side="bottom", ) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", show_row_names=False) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", row_names_gp=gpar(col=["red"] * 10 + ["blue"] * 8)) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", row_names_centered=True, column_names_centered=True) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", column_names_rot=45) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", column_names_rot=45, column_names_side="top", column_dend_side="bottom") Dimension label sides, colors, and rotation By default, row_names_max_width and column_names_max_height cap the layout space reserved for labels at 6 cm. Long names that exceed 6 cm can overlap the heatmap unless you expand the margin using max_text_width(): from complexheatmap import max_text_width mat2 = mat.copy() idx = list(mat2.index) idx[0] = "very_long_feature_identifier_example_01" mat2.index = idx Heatmap(mat2, name="mat", row_title="default row_names_max_width (6 cm)") Heatmap( mat2, name="mat", row_title="row_names_max_width = max_text_width(...)", row_names_max_width=max_text_width(mat2.index, gp=gpar(fontsize=12)), ) Default 6 cm row_names_max_width vs expanded max_text_width You can also replace displayed labels without modifying the underlying matrix via row_labels and column_labels. This supports duplicate labels, Matplotlib math strings (r"$\alpha$"), and gt_render() boxed labels: row_lbl_map = {f"row{i}": f"{chr(96 + i)}{i}" for i in range(1, 25)} col_lbl_map = {f"column{j}": f"{chr(64 + j)}{j}" for j in range(1, 25)} Heatmap( mat, name="mat", row_labels=[row_lbl_map[r] for r in mat.index], column_labels=[col_lbl_map[c] for c in mat.columns], ) greek_labels = [ r"$\alpha$", r"$\beta$", r"$\gamma$", r"$\delta$", r"$\epsilon$", r"$\zeta$", r"$\eta$", r"$\theta$", r"$\iota$", r"$\kappa$", r"$\lambda$", r"$\mu$", r"$\nu$", r"$\xi$", r"$o$", r"$\pi$", r"$\rho$", r"$\sigma$", ] Heatmap(mat, name="mat", row_labels=greek_labels) Heatmap( mat, name="mat", row_labels=gt_render(list("abcdefghijklmnopqr"), padding=unit([2, 10, 2, 10], "pt")), row_names_gp=gpar(box_col=["red", "green"] * 9), ) Custom labels, math expressions, and gt_render boxed labels

title: 2.7 Heatmap split
text: ComplexHeatmap-py splits rows and columns into sub-clusters called slices using row_km, column_km, row_split, and column_split.

title: 2.7.1 Split by k-means clustering
text: row_km and column_km partition rows or columns using k-means clustering. To stabilize stochastic k-means partitions, increase row_km_repeats / column_km_repeats for consensus k-means clustering, and set ht_opt.kmeans_seed for reproducibility. When splitting by k-means or categorical variables, a parent dendrogram is drawn over slice means and separated from within-slice child dendrograms by a dotted line (show_parent_dend_line=False hides it): ht_opt.kmeans_seed = 123 Heatmap(mat, name="mat", row_km=2) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", row_km=2, column_km=3) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", row_km=2, column_km=3, show_parent_dend_line=False) # Consensus k-means across 50 runs Heatmap(mat, name="mat", row_km=2, row_km_repeats=50, column_km=3, column_km_repeats=50) Row and column splitting via k-means clustering

title:
2.7.2 Split by categorical
variables
text: Pass a 1D list/array or a multi-column pandas.DataFrame to row_split or column_split, or combine row_split with row_km (k-means clusters are inserted as the leading split factor). You can also split using an integer row_split=2 when supplying a pre-colored Dendrogram to cut the complete tree via cut_dendrogram() / cutree(), avoiding separate parent/child dendrograms: split_df = pd.DataFrame({"s1": ["A", "B"] * 9, "s2": ["C"] * 9 + ["D"] * 9}) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", row_split=["A", "B"] * 9, column_split=["C", "D"] * 12) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", row_split=split_df) # Mix categorical split with k-means or manual row_order Heatmap(mat, name="mat", row_split=["A", "B"] * 9, row_km=2) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", row_order=list(range(17, -1, -1)), row_km=2) # Split discrete character matrix by its first column Heatmap(discrete_char, name="mat", col=colors_char, row_split=discrete_char[:, 0])

title: 2.7.3 Split by dendrogram
text: Passing a single integer to row_split or column_split cuts the global hierarchical dendrogram into that many slices: dend_r = color_branches(as_dendrogram(hclust(dist(mat))), k=2) Heatmap(mat, name="mat", cluster_rows=dend_r, row_split=2)

title: 2.7.4 Order of slices
text: By default, slice order follows hierarchical clustering of slice means. Disable slice clustering with cluster_row_slices=False / cluster_column_slices=False and pass an ordered pandas.Categorical to enforce exact slice order: r_cat = pd.Categorical(["A", "B", "C"] * 6, categories=["C", "B", "A"], ordered=True) c_cat = pd.Categorical(["a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f"] * 4, categories=["f", "e", "d", "c", "b", "a"], ordered=True) Heatmap( mat, name="mat", row_split=r_cat, column_split=c_cat, cluster_row_slices=False, cluster_column_slices=False, ) Categorical, DataFrame, explicit factor order, and dendrogram-cutree splitting

title: 2.7.5 Titles for splitting
text: When split, row_title and column_title accept: - A single template string containing %s (e.g. "cluster_%s" or "Slice: %s"), where %s is replaced by each slice’s combined label ("A,C", "A,D", etc.). - An explicit list of per-slice titles matching the number of slices (e.g. ["top_slice", "middle_top", "middle_bot", "bottom_slice"]). - A single string without %s to display one shared title across all slices, or None to hide slice titles. - A global heatmap-list title passed directly to draw(ht, row_title="Global Row Title").

title:
2.7.6 Graphic parameters for
splitting
text: Graphic parameters for slice titles and dimension names accept per-slice vectors matching the number of slices (remember to use fontface in Python gpar() rather than R’s font): ht_opt.TITLE_PADDING = unit([4, 4], "points") draw( Heatmap( mat, name="mat", row_km=2, row_title_gp=gpar(col=["red", "blue"], fontface=[1, 2]), row_names_gp=gpar(col=["green", "orange"], fontsize=[10, 14]), column_km=3, column_title_gp=gpar(fill=["red", "blue", "green"], fontface=[1, 2, 3]), column_names_gp=gpar(col=["green", "orange", "purple"], fontsize=[10, 14, 8]), ) ) ht_opt(RESET=True)

title: 2.7.7 Gaps between slices
text: row_gap and column_gap accept a single Unit or a vector of Unit values between consecutive slices. Setting row_gap=unit(0, "mm"), column_gap=unit(0, "mm"), border=True partitions the matrix with crisp grid lines.

title: 2.7.8 Split heatmap annotations
text: All attached annotations (including block annotations anno_block()) split and reorder automatically along with the heatmap slices (see Chapter 3): from complexheatmap import HeatmapAnnotation, anno_barplot, anno_block, anno_points, rowAnnotation Heatmap( mat, name="mat", row_km=2, column_km=3, top_annotation=HeatmapAnnotation( Group=anno_block(gp=gpar(fill=["#E41A1C", "#377EB8", "#4DAF4A"]), labels=["C1", "C2", "C3"], labels_gp=gpar(col="white")), foo1=np.arange(1, 25), bar1=anno_points(rng.uniform(size=24)), ), right_annotation=rowAnnotation( foo2=np.arange(18, 0, -1), bar2=anno_barplot(rng.uniform(size=18)), ), border=True, ) Split titles, per-slice gpar styling, custom slice gaps, and split annotations with anno_block

title: 2.8 Heatmap as raster image
text: Vector outputs (PDF or SVG) store a rectangle primitive for every matrix cell, which quickly becomes slow and bulky for thousands of rows or columns even though individual cells map to sub-pixel dimensions. When use_raster=True, ComplexHeatmap-py renders the color matrix via Matplotlib’s high-DPI raster imshow backend (grid_raster) while keeping dendrograms, borders, labels, and legends as crisp vector graphics. By default, use_raster activates automatically whenever a numeric/categorical matrix has more than 2000 rows (with > 10 columns) or more than 2000 columns (with > 10 rows), provided cell_fun is None. When downsampling large matrices prior to rasterization, raster_resize_mat accepts True (np.nanmean) or any reduction function mapping a 2D block to a scalar (such as np.nanmax, np.nanmin, or a custom sampler): from complexheatmap import hcl_colors mat2 = np.empty((5000, 50), dtype=float) for i in range(5000): half = np.sort(np.abs(rng.standard_normal(50)))[:25] mat2[i, :] = rng.uniform(size=50) + np.concatenate([half, half[::-1]]) * ((i + 1) / 1000.0) mat2 = mat2[::-1, :] brks = np.linspace(np.quantile(mat2, 0.01), np.quantile(mat2, 0.99), 11) col_fun2 = colorRamp2(brks, hcl_colors(11, "Spectral", rev=True)) draw(Heatmap(mat2, col=col_fun2, cluster_rows=False, cluster_columns=False, show_heatmap_legend=False, use_raster=True)) draw(Heatmap(mat2, col=col_fun2, cluster_rows=False, cluster_columns=False, show_heatmap_legend=False, use_raster=True, raster_resize_mat=np.nanmean)) draw(Heatmap(mat2, col=col_fun2, cluster_rows=False, cluster_columns=False, show_heatmap_legend=False, use_raster=True, raster_resize_mat=np.nanmax)) draw(Heatmap(mat2, col=col_fun2, cluster_rows=False, cluster_columns=False, show_heatmap_legend=False, use_raster=True, raster_resize_mat=np.nanmin)) draw(Heatmap(mat2, col=col_fun2, cluster_rows=False, cluster_columns=False, show_heatmap_legend=False, use_raster=True, raster_resize_mat=lambda sub: float(sub.flat[0]))) Comparison of use_raster and raster_resize_mat reduction modes on a 5000x50 matrix The reduction in PDF output size and rendering time is dramatic. On a 2500 × 50 matrix rendered to PDF at 100 dpi: import io, time mat_big = rng.standard_normal((2500, 50)) for flag in (False, True): t0 = time.perf_counter() ht_out = draw(Heatmap(mat_big, cluster_rows=False, cluster_columns=False, show_heatmap_legend=False, use_raster=flag), width=4, height=4, dpi=100) buf = io.BytesIO() ht_out._device.fig.savefig(buf, format="pdf") print(f"use_raster={flag}: {len(buf.getvalue()) / 1024:.1f} KB in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f}s") use_raster=False: 2791.4 KB in 6.92s use_raster=True: 80.7 KB in 0.06s

title: 2.9 Customize the heatmap body
text: Each cell in the heatmap body can be augmented or replaced entirely using cell_fun (per cell) or layer_fun (vectorized per slice). High-level modules such as OncoPrint, UpSet plot, and 3D ComplexHeatmap are built on these hooks.

title: 2.9.1 cell_fun
text: cell_fun accepts a callback with 7 positional arguments (j, i, x, y, width, height, fill): - j: 0-based column index in the original matrix (0 .. ncol - 1). - i: 0-based row index in the original matrix (0 .. nrow - 1). - x, y: Unit coordinates of the cell center inside the slice body viewport. - width, height: Unit dimensions of the cell (1 / nc_s and 1 / nr_s in "npc"). - fill: resolved hex color string of the cell. from complexheatmap import convertHeight, convertWidth, dist, grid_circle, grid_rect, grid_text, hclust small_mat = mat.iloc[:9, :9] small_arr = small_mat.to_numpy() col_fun = colorRamp2([-2, 0, 2], ["green", "white", "red"]) # 1. Text overlay in every cell Heatmap( small_mat, name="mat", col=col_fun, cell_fun=lambda j, i, x, y, w, h, fill: grid_text(f"{small_arr[i, j]:.1f}", x, y, gp=gpar(fontsize=9)), ) # 2. Positive values only across splits Heatmap( small_mat, name="mat", col=col_fun, row_km=2, column_km=2, cell_fun=lambda j, i, x, y, w, h, fill: ( grid_text(f"{small_arr[i, j]:.1f}", x, y, gp=gpar(fontsize=9)) if small_arr[i, j] > 0 else None ), ) # 3. corrplot-style correlation matrix with rect_gp=gpar(type="none") cor_mat = small_mat.corr() od = hclust(dist(cor_mat)).order cor_mat = cor_mat.iloc[od, od] cor_arr = cor_mat.to_numpy() nm = list(cor_mat.index) col_cor = colorRamp2([-1, 0, 1], ["green", "white", "red"]) def cell_cor(j, i, x, y, w, h, fill): grid_rect(x=x, y=y, width=w, height=h, gp=gpar(col="grey", fill=None)) if i == j: grid_text(nm[i], x=x, y=y, gp=gpar(fontsize=8.5)) elif i > j: r_mm = min(convertWidth(w, "mm", valueOnly=True), convertHeight(h, "mm", valueOnly=True)) * 0.45 * abs(cor_arr[i, j]) grid_circle(x=x, y=y, r=unit(r_mm, "mm"), gp=gpar(fill=col_cor(cor_arr[i, j]), col=None)) else: grid_text(f"{cor_arr[i, j]:.1f}", x=x, y=y, gp=gpar(fontsize=8.5)) Heatmap( cor_mat, name="correlation", col=col_cor, rect_gp=gpar(type="none"), cell_fun=cell_cor, cluster_rows=False, cluster_columns=False, show_row_names=False, show_column_names=False, ) cell_fun value annotations and corrplot-style correlation matrix A classic custom example renders a 19 × 19 Go game board with wood tiles, grid lines, 0-based star points (i in (3, 9, 15) and j in (3, 9, 15)), black/white stones, and a custom Legend (see Chapter 5): from complexheatmap import Legend, grid_points, grid_segments def go_cell(j, i, x, y, w, h, fill): grid_rect(x, y, w, h, gp=gpar(fill="#dcb35c", col=None)) if i == 0: grid_segments(x, y - h * 0.5, x, y, gp=gpar(col="#222222", lwd=0.8)) elif i == 18: grid_segments(x, y, x, y + h * 0.5, gp=gpar(col="#222222", lwd=0.8)) else: grid_segments(x, y - h * 0.5, x, y + h * 0.5, gp=gpar(col="#222222", lwd=0.8)) if j == 0: grid_segments(x, y, x + w * 0.5, y, gp=gpar(col="#222222", lwd=0.8)) elif j == 18: grid_segments(x - w * 0.5, y, x, y, gp=gpar(col="#222222", lwd=0.8)) else: grid_segments(x - w * 0.5, y, x + w * 0.5, y, gp=gpar(col="#222222", lwd=0.8)) if i in (3, 9, 15) and j in (3, 9, 15): grid_points(x, y, pch=16, size=unit(2, "mm")) r_mm = min(convertWidth(w, "mm", valueOnly=True), convertHeight(h, "mm", valueOnly=True)) * 0.43 if go_arr[i, j] == "W": grid_circle(x, y, r=unit(r_mm, "mm"), gp=gpar(fill="white", col="#444444", lwd=0.6)) elif go_arr[i, j] == "B": grid_circle(x, y, r=unit(r_mm, "mm"), gp=gpar(fill="black", col="black")) ht_go = Heatmap( go_mat, name="go", col={"B": "black", "W": "white"}, rect_gp=gpar(type="none"), cell_fun=go_cell, cluster_rows=False, cluster_columns=False, show_row_names=False, show_column_names=False, column_title="One famous Go game", show_heatmap_legend=False, ) lgd = Legend( title="Players", labels=["player1 (B)", "player2 (W)"], type="points", pch=16, legend_gp=gpar(col=["black", "white"]), size=unit(4.5, "mm"), background="#dcb35c", ) draw(ht_go, heatmap_legend_list=[lgd]) Go game board rendered with cell_fun and a custom Legend

title: 2.9.2 layer_fun
text: layer_fun is the vectorized counterpart of cell_fun invoked once per slice rather than once per cell. Its 7 vector arguments (j, i, x, y, w, h, fill) hold 1D arrays/Units for every cell in the current slice, and an optional 8th/9th parameter (..., slice_r, slice_c) passes the 1-based row and column slice indices. Because i and j are 0-based index arrays, use ch.pindex(mat, i, j) for pairwise lookup (mat[i[k], j[k]]): from complexheatmap import pindex, restore_matrix mfoo = np.arange(1, 10).reshape(3, 3, order="F") # array([[1, 4, 7], # [2, 5, 8], # [3, 6, 9]]) pindex(mfoo, [0, 1], [0, 2]) # array([1, 8]) When graphics depend on neighboring cells within a slice, restore_matrix(j, i, x, y) reconstructs a 2D matrix of vector positions ordered top-to-bottom and left-to-right inside the slice: # 1. Conditional slice border on off-diagonal slices def layer_slice_border(j, i, x, y, w, h, fill, slice_r, slice_c): v = pindex(small_arr, i, j) grid_text([f"{val:.1f}" for val in v], x, y, gp=gpar(fontsize=9)) if slice_r != slice_c: grid_rect(gp=gpar(lwd=2.0, col="black", fill="transparent")) # 2. Connect neighboring same-sign cells along each row using restore_matrix() def layer_neighbor(j, i, x, y, w, h, fill): ind_mat = restore_matrix(j, i, x, y) for ir in range(ind_mat.shape[0]): for ic in range(1, ind_mat.shape[1]): ind1 = int(ind_mat[ir, ic - 1]) ind2 = int(ind_mat[ir, ic]) v1 = small_arr[i[ind1], j[ind1]] v2 = small_arr[i[ind2], j[ind2]] if v1 * v2 > 0: line_col = "darkred" if v1 > 0 else "darkgreen" grid_segments(x[ind1], y[ind1], x[ind2], y[ind2], gp=gpar(col=line_col, lwd=2)) grid_points(x[[ind1, ind2]], y[[ind1, ind2]], pch=16, gp=gpar(col=line_col), size=unit(3.2, "mm")) # 3. Highlight row index 1 and column index 2 in every slice (0-based) def layer_crosshair(j, i, x, y, w, h, fill): ind_mat = restore_matrix(j, i, x, y) inds = np.unique(np.concatenate([ind_mat[1, :], ind_mat[:, 2]])) grid_points(x[inds], y[inds], pch=16, size=unit(3.6, "mm"), gp=gpar(col="black")) Vectorized layer_fun examples with pindex, slice_r/slice_c, and restore_matrix

title: 2.10 Size of the heatmap
text: width and height control the heatmap body dimensions, whereas heatmap_width and heatmap_height control the complete heatmap dimensions including dendrograms, titles, row/column names, and annotations (excluding legends): from complexheatmap import ht_size ht1 = Heatmap(mat, name="mat", width=unit(8, "cm"), height=unit(8, "cm")) ht1_drawn = draw(ht1) print(ht_size(ht1_drawn)) # unit([118.441mm, 112.999mm]) ht2 = Heatmap(mat, name="mat", heatmap_width=unit(8, "cm"), heatmap_height=unit(8, "cm")) ht2_drawn = draw(ht2) print(ht_size(ht2_drawn)) # unit([93.4762mm, 80mm]) Comparison of width/height (body) vs heatmap_width/heatmap_height (total) Notice ht_size(ht2_drawn) reports height 80 mm (8 cm) and width 93.5 mm (8 cm heatmap + legend width). Reassigning the return value of draw(ht) is essential before calling ht_size(), because layout dimensions are computed during draw().

title: 2.11 Plot the heatmap
text: Heatmap() constructs an uninitialized Heatmap specification; clustering, splitting, and layout computation happen only when draw() is executed. In Python, you can render or export a heatmap with either: ht = Heatmap(mat, name="mat") # Equivalent ways to draw or save ht_drawn = draw(ht) ht_drawn = ht.draw(save="heatmap.png", width=8, height=6, dpi=150) Calling draw(ht) creates a single-element HeatmapList and delegates to HeatmapList.draw(), which accepts global layout arguments such as heatmap_legend_side, padding, row_title, and column_title (covered in Chapter 4). In Jupyter/IPython environments, Heatmap and HeatmapList also define _repr_png_() for automatic inline display.

title:
2.12 Extract orders and
dendrograms
text: Use row_order(), column_order(), row_dend(), and column_dend() to extract clustering orderings (0-based Python indices) and Dendrogram objects. Always call ht = draw(ht) first so row_order(ht) extracts the exact ordering rendered on screen rather than recomputing clustering (especially important when row_km or column_km is used): from complexheatmap import column_dend, column_order, row_dend, row_order small_mat = mat.iloc[:9, :9] ht = Heatmap(small_mat) ht_drawn = draw(ht) print(row_order(ht_drawn)) # [4, 2, 5, 7, 1, 3, 8, 0, 6] When rows or columns are split into multiple slices, row_order(), column_order(), row_dend(), and column_dend() return a Python list with one entry per slice: ht_opt.kmeans_seed = 123 ht = Heatmap(small_mat, row_km=2, column_km=3) ht_drawn = draw(ht) print(row_order(ht_drawn)) # [[4, 2, 5], [7, 1, 3, 8, 0, 6]] print(column_order(ht_drawn)) # [[5, 1, 0], [7, 3, 8, 4], [2, 6]] print(row_dend(ht_drawn)) # [Dendrogram(members=3, height=2.557, leaf=False), Dendrogram(members=6, height=3.563, leaf=False)] print(column_dend(ht_drawn)) # [Dendrogram(members=3, height=1.859, leaf=False), Dendrogram(members=4, height=2.61, leaf=False), Dendrogram(members=2, height=2.567, leaf=False)]

title: 2.13 Subset a heatmap
text: An uninitialized Heatmap (before draw()) supports standard 0-based Python slicing, integer lists, boolean masks, and row/column name indexing via ht[rows, cols]. Attached annotations, per-element gpar vectors, and split settings (row_km, column_km, categorical splits) are subsetted automatically: from complexheatmap import dim ht = Heatmap(mat, name="mat") print(dim(ht)) # (18, 24) ht_sub = ht[:10, :10] Combining annotations, k-means splitting, and 0-based slicing (ht[:10, :10] or ht[::2, 1::2] for even-indexed rows and odd-indexed columns): ht = Heatmap( mat, name="mat", row_km=2, column_km=3, col=colorRamp2([-2, 0, 2], ["green", "white", "red"]), top_annotation=HeatmapAnnotation(foo1=np.arange(1, 25), bar1=anno_points(rng.uniform(size=24))), right_annotation=rowAnnotation(foo2=np.arange(18, 0, -1), bar2=anno_barplot(rng.uniform(size=18))), ) draw(ht[:10, :10]) draw(ht[::2, 1::2]) Subsetting a Heatmap with annotations and k-means splits preserved Subsetting works only prior to draw() and is not supported when cluster_rows/cluster_columns holds a pre-computed Dendrogram/Hclust or when cell_fun/layer_fun indexes an external unsubsetted matrix directly. Subsetting methods for HeatmapAnnotation and HeatmapList are introduced in Chapter 3 and Chapter 4.

title: 3 Heatmap Annotations
text: Heatmap annotations are essential components that display additional metadata or summary plots aligned with the rows or columns of a heatmap. ComplexHeatmap-py offers comprehensive support for built-in annotation types as well as custom graphics via AnnotationFunction. Annotations can be attached to any of the four margins of a Heatmap() using top_annotation, bottom_annotation, left_annotation, and right_annotation. Each of those four arguments accepts a HeatmapAnnotation object constructed with HeatmapAnnotation(), or rowAnnotation() for row-side annotations (rowAnnotation(...) is simply shorthand for HeatmapAnnotation(..., which="row")). Below is a quick example attaching both column and row annotations: import numpy as np import pandas as pd import complexheatmap as ch from complexheatmap import Heatmap, HeatmapAnnotation, anno_barplot, rowAnnotation rng = np.random.default_rng(123) mat = pd.DataFrame( rng.standard_normal((10, 10)), index=[f"R{i}" for i in range(1, 11)], columns=[f"C{j}" for j in range(1, 11)], ) column_ha = HeatmapAnnotation(foo1=rng.uniform(size=10), bar1=anno_barplot(rng.uniform(size=10))) row_ha = rowAnnotation(foo2=rng.uniform(size=10), bar2=anno_barplot(rng.uniform(size=10))) ht1 = Heatmap(mat, name="mat", top_annotation=column_ha, right_annotation=row_ha) ch.draw(ht1) Heatmap with top column annotation and right row annotation Or place them on the bottom and left margins instead: ht2 = Heatmap(mat, name="mat", bottom_annotation=column_ha, left_annotation=row_ha) ch.draw(ht2) Heatmap with bottom column annotation and left row annotation Above, column_ha and row_ha each combine a vector-like “simple annotation” (foo1, foo2) with a “complex annotation” (bar1, bar2 via anno_barplot()). Annotations are defined as keyword arguments (name=value). Heatmap annotations can also stand independently of a single Heatmap and be concatenated into a HeatmapList with + horizontally or %v% vertically (see A List of Heatmaps): # Code only for demonstration Heatmap(...) + rowAnnotation(...) + ... Heatmap(...) %v% HeatmapAnnotation(...) %v% ... Inspecting column_ha and row_ha prints a summary of their orientation, observation count, dimensions, and component names: print(column_ha) A HeatmapAnnotation object with 2 annotation(s) name: heatmap_annotation_1 position: column items: 10 width: 1npc height: 15.3515mm annotations: ['foo1', 'bar1'] print(row_ha) A HeatmapAnnotation object with 2 annotation(s) name: heatmap_annotation_2 position: row items: 10 width: 15.3515mm height: 1npc annotations: ['foo2', 'bar2'] In the sections that follow, we illustrate standalone annotation tracks directly using ch.draw(ha, test=True) unless a full heatmap context is needed. Column and row annotation options are symmetric: omit which (or set which="column") for column annotations, and use rowAnnotation(...) (or which="row") for row annotations. Indexing convention reminder: Vector/matrix indices passed into ComplexHeatmap-py (such as anno_mark(at=[...]), anno_link(align_to=...), and annotation subsetting ha[:5, ["foo", "bar"]]) are 0-based Python indices, whereas viewport slice numbers in decorate_annotation(..., slice=1) and list_components() are 1-based.

title: 3.1 Simple annotation
text: A “simple annotation” maps a numeric or categorical vector (or matrix/DataFrame) to colored grid cells—just like a compact 1-track heatmap. Simply pass a named vector to HeatmapAnnotation(): ha = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=np.arange(1, 11)) ch.draw(ha, test=True) Simple continuous numeric annotation Or a discrete categorical vector: bars = rng.choice(["a", "b", "c"], 10) ha = HeatmapAnnotation(bar=bars) ch.draw(ha, test=True) Simple discrete categorical annotation You can use any annotation name that does not collide with reserved HeatmapAnnotation() keyword arguments. When col is omitted, random colors are generated automatically. To specify colors explicitly, pass a dictionary col keyed by annotation name. For continuous values, provide a mapping created with colorRamp2(): from complexheatmap import colorRamp2 col_fun = colorRamp2([0, 5, 10], ["blue", "white", "red"]) ha = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=np.arange(1, 11), col={"foo": col_fun}) ch.draw(ha, test=True) Simple continuous annotation with explicit colorRamp2 mapping For discrete annotations, supply a dictionary mapping each category level to a color: disc_col = {"a": "red", "b": "green", "c": "blue"} ha = HeatmapAnnotation(bar=bars, col={"bar": disc_col}) ch.draw(ha, test=True) Simple discrete annotation with explicit level colors Multiple simple annotations can be combined in one HeatmapAnnotation() call, with col containing one entry per annotation name. Values in col are also reused to generate the annotation legends automatically: ha = HeatmapAnnotation( foo=np.arange(1, 11), bar=bars, col={"foo": col_fun, "bar": disc_col}, ) ch.draw(ha, test=True) Multiple simple annotations with shared col dictionary Missing values (np.nan / None) are colored via na_col: foo_na = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, np.nan, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10], dtype=float) bar_na = [None] + list(rng.choice(["a", "b", "c"], 9)) ha = HeatmapAnnotation( foo=foo_na, bar=bar_na, col={"foo": col_fun, "bar": disc_col}, na_col="black", ) ch.draw(ha, test=True) Simple annotations with na_col=‘black’ for missing entries gp controls graphical parameters such as grid cell borders: from complexheatmap import gpar ha = HeatmapAnnotation( foo=np.arange(1, 11), bar=bars, col={"foo": col_fun, "bar": disc_col}, gp=gpar(col="black"), ) ch.draw(ha, test=True) Simple annotations with cell borders set via gp A simple annotation can also be a 2D matrix or pandas.DataFrame whose columns share a single color scale. Columns of the input DataFrame/matrix become stacked rows in a column annotation (with DataFrame column names used as individual row labels): df_mat = pd.DataFrame({"a": rng.uniform(size=10), "b": rng.uniform(size=10)}) ha = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=df_mat) ch.draw(ha, test=True) Simple matrix/DataFrame annotation with named tracks When an unnamed NumPy 2D array is passed, the annotation keyword name (foo) is centered across the tracks: ha = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=np.column_stack([rng.uniform(size=10), rng.uniform(size=10)])) ch.draw(ha, test=True) Simple unnamed 2D array annotation If you already hold an annotation table as a pandas.DataFrame, pass it directly via df=: anno_df = pd.DataFrame({"foo": np.arange(1, 11), "bar": bars}) ha = HeatmapAnnotation(df=anno_df, col={"foo": col_fun, "bar": disc_col}) ch.draw(ha, test=True) Simple annotations constructed from a DataFrame via df= df= can be mixed with additional individual keyword annotations (which are appended after the df columns): ha = HeatmapAnnotation( df=anno_df, foo2=rng.standard_normal(10), col={"foo": col_fun, "bar": disc_col}, ) ch.draw(ha, test=True) Mixing df= table annotations with extra keyword annotations border=True draws an outer border around each annotation track: ha = HeatmapAnnotation( foo=np.column_stack([np.arange(1, 11), np.arange(10, 0, -1)]), bar=bars, col={"foo": col_fun, "bar": disc_col}, border=True, ) ch.draw(ha, test=True) Simple annotations with outer track borders simple_anno_size controls the height (for column annotations) or width (for row annotations)

title:
3.2 Simple annotation
as an annotation function
text: Complex annotations are built with anno_*() factory functions, which return an AnnotationFunction object. When passed inside HeatmapAnnotation() or rowAnnotation(), every anno_*() function automatically detects whether it is in a column or row annotation environment—so you rarely need to specify which= manually. Simple annotations are created internally by anno_simple(). Calling anno_simple() directly does not generate legends automatically, though custom legends can still be constructed manually (see Legends): # Code only for demonstration ha = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=np.arange(1, 11)) # Internally equivalent to: ha = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_simple(np.arange(1, 11))) The main advantage of calling anno_simple() explicitly is adding point symbols or single-character markers (pch) on top of the colored cells, styled via pt_gp and pt_size: from complexheatmap import anno_simple ha = HeatmapAnnotation( foo=anno_simple(np.arange(1, 11), pch=[1] * 10, pt_gp=gpar(col="red"), pt_size=unit(np.arange(1, 11), "mm")) ) ch.draw(ha, test=True) anno_simple() with varying point sizes pch can be a numeric symbol vector: ha = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_simple(np.arange(1, 11), pch=list(range(1, 11)))) ch.draw(ha, test=True) anno_simple() with a vector of pch marker codes Or a vector of single-character labels: ha = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_simple(np.arange(1, 11), pch=rng.choice(["a", "b", "c"], 10).tolist())) ch.draw(ha, test=True) anno_simple() with letter symbols in pch Entries set to None (or np.nan) leave that cell unmarked: ha = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_simple(np.arange(1, 11), pch=[1, 2, 3, 4, None, 6, 7, 8, None, 10])) ch.draw(ha, test=True) anno_simple() skipping cells where pch is None When the input to anno_simple() is a 2D matrix, pch can match either the columns, rows, or full 2D matrix shape: mat2 = np.column_stack([np.arange(1, 11), np.arange(10, 0, -1)]) # Matching matrix shape across columns ha = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_simple(mat2, pch=np.tile([1, 2], (10, 1)))) ch.draw(ha, test=True) 2D anno_simple() with column-wise pch # Matching matrix rows ha = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_simple(mat2, pch=np.arange(1, 11))) ch.draw(ha, test=True) 2D anno_simple() with row-wise pch # Full 2D pch matrix with missing entries pch_mat = np.arange(1, 21, dtype=object).reshape(10, 2) pch_mat.ravel()[rng.choice(20, 10, replace=False)] = None ha = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_simple(mat2, pch=pch_mat)) ch.draw(ha, test=True) 2D anno_simple() with a sparse 2D pch matrix Because anno_simple() does not emit legends automatically, you can attach custom Legend() objects via annotation_legend_list in ch.draw() (see Legends). Below, we map -log10(pvalue) to color and overlay * for p < 0.01: from complexheatmap import Legend pvalue = 10.0 ** (-rng.uniform(0, 3, 10)) is_sig = pvalue < 0.01 pch_sig = ["*" if s else None for s in is_sig] pvalue_col_fun = colorRamp2([0, 2, 3], ["green", "white", "red"]) ha_pv = HeatmapAnnotation( pvalue=anno_simple(-np.log10(pvalue), col=pvalue_col_fun, pch=pch_sig), annotation_name_side="left", ) ht_pv = Heatmap(rng.standard_normal((10, 10)), name="mat", top_annotation=ha_pv) lgd_pvalue = Legend(title="p-value", col_fun=pvalue_col_fun, at=[0, 1, 2, 3], labels=["1", "0.1", "0.01", "0.001"]) lgd_sig = Legend(pch="*", type="points", labels=["< 0.01"]) ch.draw(ht_pv, annotation_legend_list=[lgd_pvalue, lgd_sig]) Combining anno_simple() significance stars with manual p-value legends Inside anno_simple(), height/width sets the total track size, whereas simple_anno_size sets the thickness per row/column of a multi-track matrix (ignored if height/width is explicitly set): ha1 = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_simple(np.arange(1, 11), height=unit(2, "cm"))) ch.draw(ha1, test=True) ha2 = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_simple(mat2, simple_anno_size=unit(2, "cm"))) ch.draw(ha2, test=True) Setting total height directly inside anno_simple() Setting per-row simple_anno_size inside 2D anno_simple() For all anno_*() functions introduced below, c

title: 3.3 Empty annotation
text: anno_empty() reserves a blank annotation region that you can later populate using decorate_annotation() (see Heatmap Decoration): from complexheatmap import anno_empty ha = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_empty(border=True)) ch.draw(ha, index=list(range(10)), test=True) Blank placeholder created by anno_empty(border=True) A common application is highlighting summary keywords for each cluster slice beside a k-means-split heatmap. Note that decorate_annotation("foo", slice=i) uses 1-based slice indices (1..4): from complexheatmap import decorate_annotation, grid_rect, grid_text, max_text_width def random_text(n): letters = list("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz") return ["".join(rng.choice(letters, int(rng.integers(4, 11)))) for _ in range(n)] text_list = [random_text(4) for _ in range(4)] flat_txt = [w for grp in text_list for w in grp] ha = rowAnnotation(foo=anno_empty(border=False, width=max_text_width(flat_txt) + unit(4, "mm"))) ht = Heatmap(rng.standard_normal((100, 10)), name="mat", row_km=4, right_annotation=ha) ch.draw(ht) for i in range(1, 5): with decorate_annotation("foo", slice=i): grid_rect(x=0, width=unit(2, "mm"), gp=gpar(fill=i, col=None), just="left") grid_text("\n".join(text_list[i - 1]), x=unit(4, "mm"), just="left") Decorating row-split slices inside anno_empty() Note that this pattern can also be created directly with anno_block() or anno_textbox() (Text box annotation). You can also treat anno_empty() as a custom plotting canvas, remembering to reorder your data vector by column_order(ht) (0-based indices) before plotting: from complexheatmap import Viewport, column_order, grid_lines, grid_points, popViewport, pushViewport ha_pts = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_empty(border=True, height=unit(3, "cm"))) ht_pts = Heatmap(rng.standard_normal((10, 10)), name="mat", top_annotation=ha_pts) res = ch.draw(ht_pts) co = column_order(res) value = rng.uniform(size=10) with decorate_annotation("foo"): x_pos = np.arange(1, 11) val_ord = value[co] pushViewport(Viewport(xscale=(0.5, 10.5), yscale=(0, 1))) grid_lines([0.5, 10.5], [0.5, 0.5], gp=gpar(lty=2), default_units="native") grid_points( x_pos, val_ord, pch=16, size=unit(2, "mm"), gp=gpar(col=["red" if v > 0.5 else "blue" for v in val_ord]), default_units="native", ) ch.grid_yaxis(at=[0, 0.5, 1]) popViewport() Custom scatter plot with reference line inside anno_empty()

title: 3.4 Block annotation
text: anno_block() draws colored blocks aligned to split heatmap slices—either as labeled group banners or as virtual plotting panels for custom slice-level graphics.

title: 3.4.1 Block for putting labels
text: When rows or columns are split, anno_block() draws one rectangle per slice: from complexheatmap import anno_block m10 = rng.standard_normal((10, 10)) ch.draw( Heatmap( m10, name="mat", top_annotation=HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_block(gp=gpar(fill=[2, 3, 4]))), column_km=3, ) ) Basic colored block annotations matching column k-means slices Add slice labels via labels and labels_gp (matching the number of slices): ch.draw( Heatmap( m10, name="mat", top_annotation=HeatmapAnnotation( foo=anno_block( gp=gpar(fill=[2, 3, 4]), labels=["group1", "group2", "group3"], labels_gp=gpar(col="white", fontsize=10), ) ), column_km=3, left_annotation=rowAnnotation( foo=anno_block( gp=gpar(fill=[2, 3, 4]), labels=["group1", "group2", "group3"], labels_gp=gpar(col="white", fontsize=10), ) ), row_km=3, ) ) Labeled block annotations on both column and row slices To draw higher-level group banners spanning multiple slices, reserve space above the slice blocks with anno_empty(border=False), draw the heatmap, locate the slice viewports with seekViewport(), and draw a spanning rectangle and label inside "global": mat2 = rng.standard_normal((50, 50)) split = np.repeat(np.arange(1, 6), 10) ha = HeatmapAnnotation( empty=anno_empty(border=False), foo=anno_block(gp=gpar(fill=list(range(2, 7))), labels=list("ABCDE")), ) ch.draw(Heatmap(mat2, name="mat2", column_split=split, top_annotation=ha, column_title=None)) Allocating an anno_empty() header above five anno_block() slices Every annotation slice viewport follows the naming pattern annotation_{annotation_name}_{slice_index} (1-based slice_index). You can inspect all registered viewport names with list_components() and measure their coordinates in millimeters relative to "global" via seekViewport(): from complexheatmap import seekViewport vp1 = seekViewport("annotation_empty_1") vp2 = seekViewport("annotation_empty_3") vp_glob = seekViewport("global") x0 = unit(vp1.x0_mm - vp_glob.x0_mm, "mm") y0 = unit(vp1.y0_mm - vp_glob.y0_mm, "mm") w = unit((vp2.x0_mm + vp2.w_mm) - vp1.x0_mm, "mm") h = unit((vp2.y0_mm + vp2.h_mm) - vp1.y0_mm, "mm") grid_rect(x0, y0, width=w, height=h, just=["left", "bottom"], gp=gpar(fill="red")) grid_text("group 1", x=x0 + w * 0.5, y=y0 + h * 0.5, gp=gpar(col="white")) Drawing a multi-slice header rectangle over slices 1 to 3 Wrapping this into a helper group_block_anno() lets you label arbitrary groups of consecutive slices cleanly: def group_block_anno(group, empty_anno, gp_box=None, label=None, label_gp=None): vp1 = seekViewport(f"annotation_{empty_anno}_{min(group)}") vp2 = seekViewport(f"annotation_{empty_anno}_{max(group)}") vp_glob = seekViewport("global") x0 = unit(vp1.x0_mm - vp_glob.x0_mm, "mm") y0 = unit(vp1.y0_mm - vp_glob.y0_mm, "mm") w = unit((vp2.x0_mm + vp2.w_mm) - vp1.x0_mm, "mm") h = unit((vp2.y0_mm + vp2.h_mm) - vp1.y0_mm, "mm") grid_rect(x0, y0, width=w, height=h, just=["left", "bottom"], gp=gp_box or gpar()) if label is not None: grid_text(label, x=x0 + w * 0.5, y=y0 + h * 0.5, gp=label_gp or gpar()) ha = HeatmapAnnotation( empty=anno_empty(border=False, height=unit(8, "mm")), foo=anno_block(gp=gpar(fill=list(range(2, 7))), labels=list("ABCDE")), ) ch.draw(Heatmap(mat2, name="mat2", column_split=split, top_annotation=ha, column_title=None)) group_block_anno([1, 2, 3], "empty", gp_box=gpar(fill="red"), label="group 1", label_gp=gpar(col="white")) group_block_anno([4, 5], "empty", gp_box=gpar(fill="blue"), label="group 2", label_gp=gpar(col="white")) Spanning multi-slice group headers over slices 1-3 and 4-5

title: 3.4.2 Blocks as plotting regions
text: When panel_fun is passed to anno_block(), each block acts as an independent plotting viewport. panel_fun(index, levels) receives two arguments: index: 0-based row/column indices belonging to the current slice. levels: the split level(s) identifying the slice (a scalar or sequence when combining multiple split variables such as row_km + row_split). When panel_fun is provided, default fill/label parameters on anno_block() are ignored: col_map = {"1": "red", "2": "blue", "A": "green", "B": "orange"} def _pf(index, levels): lv = [str(levels)] if isinstance(levels, str) else [str(v) for v in levels] grid_rect(gp=gpar(fill=col_map.get(lv[-1], "grey"), col="black")) txt = ",".join(lv) + f"\n{len(index)} rows" grid_text(txt, 0.5, 0.5, rot=0, gp=gpar(col=col_map.get(lv[0], "black"))) ch.draw( Heatmap(m10, name="mat", row_km=2, row_split=rng.choice(["A", "B"], 10)) + rowAnnotation(foo=anno_block(panel_fun=_pf, width=unit(3, "cm"))) ) Custom graphics rendered per slice inside anno_block(panel_fun=…) align_to lets you draw blocks only for selected subsets of contiguous 0-based indices (either alongside row_split or on an unclustered heatmap): sp_ab = rng.choice(["A", "B"], 10) align_a = {"A": [i for i, v in enumerate(sp_ab) if v == "A"]} def _pf_count(index, nm): grid_rect() grid_text(f"{len(index)} rows", 0.5, 0.5) ch.draw( Heatmap(m10, name="mat", row_split=sp_ab) + rowAnnotation(foo=anno_block(align_to=align_a, panel_fun=_pf_count, width=unit(3, "cm"))) ) Drawing an anno_block() panel for only slice A via align_to Even without row_split, align_to can target any contiguous 0-based row range when cluster_rows=False: ch.draw( Heatmap(m10, name="mat", cluster_rows=False) + rowAnnotation(foo=anno_block(align_to={"A": [1, 2, 3], "B": [6, 7, 8]}, panel_fun=_pf_count, width=unit(3, "cm"))) ) Aligning anno_block() panels to contiguous index ranges without splitting

title: 3.5 Image annotation
text: anno_image() places local image files (PNG, JPEG, TIFF, SVG, etc., or NumPy RGBA arrays) into each annotation cell: from complexheatmap import anno_image ha = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_image(icon_paths)) ch.draw(ha, test=True) Image annotation rendering PNG icons in each cell Use gp to assign cell background colors (visible behind transparent pixels) and borders: ha = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_image(icon_paths, gp=gpar(fill=list(range(1, 11)), col="black"))) ch.draw(ha, test=True) Image annotation with per-cell background fill and border border sets the outer border color of the annotation track, and space adds inner padding around each image: ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_image(icon_paths, border="red")), test=True) ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_image(icon_paths, space=unit(3, "mm"))), test=True) Image annotation with outer red border Image annotation with 3 mm cell padding via space= Elements set to "" or None leave those cells blank: partial = ["", ""] + list(icon_paths[2:]) ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_image(partial)), test=True) Image annotation skipping empty-string entries

title: 3.6 Points annotation
text: anno_points() plots numeric values as scatter points. It accepts a 1D vector or a 2D matrix (where rows correspond to observations along the heatmap axis and columns form multiple point series styled by pch, size, and gp): from complexheatmap import anno_points ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_points(rng.uniform(size=10))), test=True) ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_points(rng.uniform(size=(10, 2)), pch=[1, 2], gp=gpar(col=[2, 3]))), test=True) Points annotation from a 1D numeric vector Points annotation from a 2-column matrix with distinct pch and colors ylim fixes the data axis range, extend adds axis padding, axis toggles axis visibility, and axis_param customizes ticks, labels, side, and rotation. Inspect default axis settings with default_axis_param(): from complexheatmap import default_axis_param default_axis_param("column") # {'at': None, 'labels': None, 'labels_rot': 0, 'gp': {'fontsize': 8}, 'side': 'left', 'facing': 'outside', 'direction': 'normal'} Override any subset of axis_param: ha = HeatmapAnnotation( foo=anno_points( rng.uniform(size=10), ylim=(0, 1), axis_param={"side": "right", "at": [0, 0.5, 1], "labels": ["zero", "half", "one"]}, ) ) ch.draw(ha, test=True) Points annotation with custom right-side axis ticks and labels For row annotations, you can rotate axis labels with labels_rot: ha = rowAnnotation( foo=anno_points( rng.uniform(size=10), which="row", ylim=(0, 1), width=unit(2, "cm"), axis_param={"side": "bottom", "at": [0, 0.5, 1], "labels": ["zero", "half", "one"], "labels_rot": 45}, ) ) ch.draw(ha, test=True) Row points annotation with 45-degree rotated axis labels Axis configuration via axis and axis_param works identically across all other axis-bearing annotation functions. Control the annotation height (or width for row annotations) directly inside anno_points() (default height is 1 cm / 5 mm depending on context): ha = HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_points(rng.uniform(size=10), height=unit(2, "cm"))) ch.draw(ha, test=True) Points annotation with custom height=2cm

title: 3.7 Line annotation
text: anno_lines() connects sequential values with line segments and accepts either a 1D vector or a 2D matrix: from complexheatmap import anno_lines ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_lines(rng.uniform(size=10))), test=True) mat_l = np.column_stack([np.tile(np.arange(1, 6), 2), np.tile(np.arange(5, 0, -1), 2)]) ch.draw( HeatmapAnnotation( foo=anno_lines(mat_l, gp=gpar(col=[2, 3]), add_points=True, pt_gp=gpar(col=[5, 6]), pch=[1, 16]) ), test=True, ) Line annotation from a 1D vector Multi-series line annotation with overlaid points Setting smooth=True fits a smoothed curve (enabling add_points=True by default). Keep in mind that smoothing fits along the displayed (potentially clustered) order: ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_lines(rng.uniform(size=10), smooth=True)), test=True) Line annotation with smooth=True As with anno_points(), pass height= or width= directly to anno_lines() to resize it.

title: 3.8 Barplot annotation
text: anno_barplot() represents values as vertical or horizontal bars and shares ylim, axis, and axis_param with anno_points(): ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_barplot(np.arange(1, 11))), test=True) Basic barplot annotation bar_width sets the bar width as a fraction of the cell width (from 0 to 1), and gp sets fill and border colors: ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_barplot(np.arange(1, 11), bar_width=1)), test=True) ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_barplot(np.arange(1, 11), gp=gpar(fill=list(range(1, 11))))), test=True) Barplot annotation with bar_width=1 Barplot annotation with per-bar fill colors baseline sets where bars originate—either "min" or a numeric baseline such as 0: ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_barplot(np.arange(-5, 6), baseline="min")), test=True) ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_barplot(np.arange(-5, 6), baseline=0)), test=True) Signed barplot annotation with baseline=‘min’ Signed barplot annotation with baseline=0 When given a 2D matrix, anno_barplot() draws stacked bars by default, with gp elements matching the matrix columns: mat_b = np.column_stack([np.arange(1, 11), np.arange(10, 0, -1)]) ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_barplot(mat_b)), test=True) ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_barplot(mat_b, gp=gpar(fill=[2, 3], col=[2, 3]))), test=True) Default stacked barplot annotation from a 2-column matrix Stacked barplot annotation with custom column colors A common use case is visualizing row-normalized proportions: m_prop = rng.uniform(size=(10, 4)) m_prop = m_prop / m_prop.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True) ch.draw( HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_barplot(m_prop, gp=gpar(fill=[2, 3, 4, 5]), bar_width=1, height=unit(6, "cm"))), test=True, ) Stacked proportion barplot annotation For left-side row barplots, set axis_param={"direction": "reverse"} so bars grow leftward from the heatmap boundary: ha_rev = ( rowAnnotation( axis_reverse=anno_barplot( m_prop, gp=gpar(fill=[2, 3, 4, 5]), axis_param={"direction": "reverse"}, bar_width=1, width=unit(4, "cm") ) ) + rowAnnotation(axis_normal=anno_barplot(m_prop, gp=gpar(fill=[2, 3, 4, 5]), bar_width=1, width=unit(4, "cm"))) ) ch.draw(ha_rev, ht_gap=unit(4, "mm")) Comparing reversed and normal row barplot directions Pass add_numbers=True to print each bar’s value next to it: ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_barplot(np.arange(1, 11), add_numbers=True, height=unit(1, "cm"))), test=True) Barplot annotation with numeric labels via add_numbers=True For multi-column inputs, beside=True places grouped bars side by side, and attach=True eliminates the inner gap between bars in the same group: ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_barplot(mat_b, beside=True)), test=True) ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_barplot(mat_b, beside=True, attach=True)), test=True) Grouped side-by-side barplot annotation via beside=True Grouped barplot with touching bars via attach=True

title: 3.9 Boxplot annotation
text: anno_boxplot() summarizes distributions across columns (for column annotations) or rows (for row annotations) from a matrix or list of vectors, and works best when the number of heatmaps columns/rows is modest: from complexheatmap import anno_boxplot rng_bp = np.random.default_rng(12345) m = rng_bp.standard_normal((10, 10)) ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_boxplot(m, height=unit(4, "cm"))), test=True) ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_boxplot(m, height=unit(4, "cm"), gp=gpar(fill=list(range(1, 11))))), test=True) ch.draw(HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_boxplot(m, height=unit(4, "cm"), box_width=0.9, outline=False)), test=True) Default column boxplot annotation Boxplot annotation with per-box fill colors Boxplot annotation with box_width=0.9 and outline=False anno_boxplot() renders one boxplot per column or row. See Add multiple boxplots for single row for drawing multiple boxplots in a single row, and Zoom/link annotation for summarizing groups of rows.

title: 3.10 Histogram annotation
text: anno_histogram() is usually placed as a row annotation and computes histograms per row (or per column for column annotations) from a matrix or list of vectors: from complexheatmap import anno_histogram m = rng.standard_normal((10, 100)) ch.draw(rowAnnotation(foo=anno_histogram(m)), test=True) ch.draw(rowAnnotation(foo=anno_histogram(m, n_breaks=20)), test=True) ch.draw(rowAnnotation(foo=anno_histogram(m, gp=gpar(fill=list(range(1, 11))))), test=True) Row histogram annotation with default binning Row histogram annotation with n_breaks=20 Row histogram annotation with per-row fill colors

title: 3.11 Density annotation
text: anno_density() displays kernel density estimates for each row or column: from complexheatmap import anno_density ch.draw(rowAnnotation(foo=anno_density(m)), test=True) Default density curve row annotation Increase joyplot_scale with semi-transparent fill to create overlapping ridge/joyplot peaks, or set type="violin" for violin plots: ch.draw(rowAnnotation(foo=anno_density(m, joyplot_scale=2, gp=gpar(fill="#CCCCCC80"))), test=True) ch.draw(rowAnnotation(foo=anno_density(m, type="violin", gp=gpar(fill=list(range(1, 11))))), test=True) Density annotation styled as overlapping ridge peaks Violin-style density annotation via type=‘violin’ When there are many rows, type="heatmap" encodes each density profile as a color strip (customizable via heatmap_colors). See also densityHeatmap() in Density heatmap: m2 = rng.standard_normal((50, 10)) ch.draw(rowAnnotation(foo=anno_density(m2, type="heatmap", width=unit(6, "cm"))), test=True) ch.draw( rowAnnotation(foo=anno_density(m2, type="heatmap", width=unit(6, "cm"), heatmap_colors=["white", "orange"])), test=True, ) Heatmap-style density annotation for 50 rows Heatmap-style density annotation with custom white-to-orange gradient

title: 3.12 Joyplot annotation
text: anno_joyplot() renders stacked ridgeline curves from either: A 2D matrix (always interpreted column-wise, with row indices 0..nrow-1 as x), or A list of 2-column DataFrames with x and y coordinates. from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde from complexheatmap import anno_joyplot m1 = rng.standard_normal((100, 10)) gx = np.linspace(-4, 4, 200) lt1 = [pd.DataFrame({"x": gx, "y": gaussian_kde(m1[:, j])(gx)}) for j in range(m1.shape[1])] ch.draw( rowAnnotation(foo=anno_joyplot(lt1, width=unit(4, "cm"), gp=gpar(fill=list(range(1, 11))), transparency=0.75)), test=True, ) Filled ridgeline annotation via anno_joyplot() Set gp=gpar(fill=None) and increase scale to draw crisp overlapping outlines: m2 = rng.standard_normal((100, 50)) lt2 = [pd.DataFrame({"x": gx, "y": gaussian_kde(m2[:, j])(gx)}) for j in range(m2.shape[1])] ch.draw(rowAnnotation(foo=anno_joyplot(lt2, width=unit(4, "cm"), gp=gpar(fill=None), scale=4)), test=True) 50-track line-only ridgeline annotation via anno_joyplot()

title: 3.13 Horizon chart annotation
text: anno_horizon() draws compact horizon charts (row annotations only) using the same input structure as anno_joyplot(), normalizing each track by x / max(abs(x)): from complexheatmap import anno_horizon lt = [np.cumprod(1 + rng.uniform(-x / 100.0, x / 100.0, 1000)) - 1.0 for x in range(1, 21)] ch.draw(rowAnnotation(foo=anno_horizon(lt)), test=True) Default horizon chart row annotation Customize positive/negative fills globally or per track via pos_fill and neg_fill in gpar(), control negative reflection via negative_from_top, and add spacing via gap: ch.draw(rowAnnotation(foo=anno_horizon(lt, gp=gpar(pos_fill="orange", neg_fill="darkgreen"))), test=True) ch.draw( rowAnnotation( foo=anno_horizon( lt, gp=gpar(pos_fill=np.repeat(["orange", "red"], 10), neg_fill=np.repeat(["darkgreen", "blue"], 10)), ) ), test=True, ) ch.draw(rowAnnotation(foo=anno_horizon(lt, negative_from_top=True)), test=True) ch.draw(rowAnnotation(foo=anno_horizon(lt, gap=unit(1, "mm"))), test=True) Horizon chart with orange positive and darkgreen negative fills Horizon chart with per-row color vectors Horizon chart with negative_from_top=True Horizon chart with 1 mm gap between tracks

title: 3.14 Text annotation
text:
anno_text() draws text labels aligned to rows or columns, styled via gp, positioned via location and just, and rotated via rot: from complexheatmap import anno_text month_names = [ "January", "February", "March", "April", "May", "June", "July", "August", "September", "October", "November", "December", ] ch.draw(rowAnnotation(foo=anno_text(month_names, gp=gpar(fontsize=[i + 5 for i in range(12)]))), test=True) ch.draw( rowAnnotation( foo=anno_text(month_names, location=1, rot=30, just="right", gp=gpar(fontsize=[i + 5 for i in range(12)])) ), test=True, ) ch.draw(rowAnnotation(foo=anno_text(month_names, location=0.5, just="center")), test=True) Text annotation with varying font sizes Text annotation with right alignment and 30-degree rotation Centered text annotation location and just are automatically adapted when attached to a heatmap margin (left-aligned on the right margin, right-aligned on the left margin), and width/height are automatically measured from text extents. Add background boxes via fill, col, and border inside gpar(): ch.draw( rowAnnotation( foo=anno_text( month_names, location=0.5, just="center", gp=gpar(fill=np.repeat([2, 3, 4], 4), col="white", border="black"), width=max_text_width(month_names) * 1.2, ) ), test=True, ) Text annotation with colored background boxes and borders Rich inline text (**bold**, *italic*,
, ...) is supported via gt_render() (see Rich text with gt_render): from complexheatmap import gt_render rich_txt = [ f"**{ch_l}** *{ch_l.lower()}* {ch_l}" for ch_l in "ABCDEFGHIJ" ] ch.draw( rowAnnotation( foo=anno_text( gt_render(rich_txt, align_widths=True, r=unit(2, "pt"), padding=unit([2, 2, 2, 2], "pt")), gp=gpar(box_col="blue", box_lwd=2), just="right", location=unit(1, "npc"), ) ), test=True, ) Styled rich-text annotation using gt_render() Unlike other annotations, anno_text() hides its annotation name by default; enable it with show_name=True: m = rng.standard_normal((10, 10)) ch.draw( Heatmap(m) + rowAnnotation( month=anno_text(month_names[:10], just="center", location=unit(0.5, "npc"), show_name=True), annotation_name_rot=0, ) ) Displaying an anno_text() title via show_name=True

title: 3.15 Numeric labels annotation
text: anno_numeric() combines formatted numbers with proportional horizontal background bars (row annotations only): from complexheatmap import anno_numeric x = np.round(rng.uniform(size=10), 3) idx = list(range(10)) ch.draw(rowAnnotation(numeric=anno_numeric(x), annotation_name_rot=0), index=idx, test=True) ch.draw(rowAnnotation(numeric=anno_numeric(x, bg_gp=gpar(fill="orange", col="black")), annotation_name_rot=0), index=idx, test=True) ch.draw( rowAnnotation(numeric=anno_numeric(x, bg_gp=gpar(fill="orange", col="black"), align_to="right"), annotation_name_rot=0), index=idx, test=True, ) ch.draw( rowAnnotation(numeric=anno_numeric(x, labels_format=lambda v: [f"{val * 100:.2f}%" for val in v]), annotation_name_rot=0), index=idx, test=True, ) Default anno_numeric() bar-backed labels anno_numeric() with orange fill and black border anno_numeric() aligned to the right anno_numeric() with percentage label formatting For vectors containing both negative and positive values, anno_numeric() centers bars around 0, and bg_gp accepts 2-element lists (or per-observation vectors) styling negative vs. positive values: x_div = np.round(rng.uniform(-1, 1, 10), 3) div_cols = ["green" if v < 0 else "red" for v in x_div] ch.draw(rowAnnotation(numeric=anno_numeric(x_div, bg_gp=gpar(fill=div_cols, col=div_cols)), annotation_name_rot=0), index=idx, test=True) Diverging anno_numeric() annotation for signed values To plot p-values on a -log10 bar scale while keeping scientific notation labels, use x_convert and labels_format: x_pv = 10.0 ** (-rng.uniform(1, 6, 10)) ch.draw( rowAnnotation( pvalue=anno_numeric( x_pv, rg=(float(x_pv.min()), 1.0), x_convert=lambda v: -np.log10(v), labels_format=lambda v: [f"{val:.2e}" for val in v], ), annotation_name_rot=0, ), index=idx, test=True, ) p-value anno_numeric() using x_convert=-log10(x) and scientific labels

title:
3.16 Completely customized
annotation
text: anno_customize() takes a categorical vector and a dictionary graphics mapping each category level to a drawing callback (x, y, w, h) giving the cell center and size: from PIL import Image from complexheatmap import anno_customize, grid_raster x = ["a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "b", "c", "c", "d", "d"] icon_arr = np.asarray(Image.open(icon_path).convert("RGBA")) graphics = { "a": lambda px, py, w, h: grid_rect(px, py, w * 0.8, h * 0.33, gp=gpar(fill="red")), "b": lambda px, py, w, h: grid_text("A", px, py, gp=gpar(col="darkgreen")), "c": lambda px, py, w, h: grid_points(px, py, gp=gpar(col="orange"), pch=16), "d": lambda px, py, w, h: grid_raster( icon_arr, px, py, width=unit(0.8, "snpc"), height=unit(0.8, "snpc") * icon_arr.shape[0] / icon_arr.shape[1] ), } m = rng.standard_normal((10, 10)) ch.draw( Heatmap( m, name="mat", top_annotation=HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_customize(x, graphics=graphics)), right_annotation=rowAnnotation(bar=anno_customize(x, graphics=graphics)), ) ) Custom per-category cell graphics via anno_customize() Reordering and row/column splitting automatically propagate to anno_customize(): ch.draw( Heatmap( m, name="mat", top_annotation=HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_customize(x, graphics=graphics)), right_annotation=rowAnnotation(bar=anno_customize(x, graphics=graphics)), column_split=x, row_split=x, ) ) anno_customize() automatically respects row_split and column_split Because Legend() also accepts graphics=, you can construct matching custom legends directly (see Legends): ht = Heatmap(m, name="mat", top_annotation=HeatmapAnnotation(foo=anno_customize(x, graphics=graphics))) lgd = Legend(title="foo", at=list(graphics.keys()), graphics=graphics) ch.draw(ht, annotation_legend_list=lgd) Adding a matching custom graphics legend for anno_customize()

title: 3.17 Mark annotation
text: anno_mark() highlights selected rows or columns with connector lines leading to non-overlapping text labels. at expects 0-based integer indices into the original matrix, and labels provides their display strings.
